lead: In a gas absorber, a solute leaves the gas film and enters the liquid film. Chapter 2.1 gave one coefficient for each film. Plant calculations need one coefficient for the whole gas phase or whole liquid phase, because the interface composition is hard to measure. The individual coefficients add as resistances in series. That gives Ky based on gas mole fraction and Kx based on liquid mole fraction. The same numbers tell whether the gas film or the liquid film controls the rate.
prereq: You need the individual coefficient kc from Chapter 2.1 and the interface equilibrium idea from Chapter 2.6.

blocks.text: In the gas film the driving force is y − y<sub>i</sub>; in the liquid film it is x<sub>i</sub> − x. At steady state the flux N<sub>A</sub> is the same through both films. Define k<sub>y</sub> = N<sub>A</sub>/(y − y<sub>i</sub>) and k<sub>x</sub> = N<sub>A</sub>/(x<sub>i</sub> − x). k<sub>y</sub> is the gas-film coefficient, kmol/(m²·s). k<sub>x</sub> is the liquid-film coefficient, kmol/(m²·s). The interface is in equilibrium, y<sub>i</sub> = m x<sub>i</sub>, where m is the slope of y* = m x. The interface itself has no storage. The composition change is split between the two films. The interface composition cannot be sampled in a plant, so calculations use bulk compositions. K<sub>y</sub> is the overall gas coefficient: N<sub>A</sub> = K<sub>y</sub>(y − y*), where y* = m x is the gas composition in equilibrium with the bulk liquid. K<sub>x</sub> is the overall liquid coefficient: N<sub>A</sub> = K<sub>x</sub>(x* − x), where x* = y/m is the liquid composition in equilibrium with the bulk gas. K<sub>y</sub> and K<sub>x</sub> are bookkeeping devices. They put both film resistances on one driving-force basis.

Add the two film drops on the gas basis. Across the gas film, y − y<sub>i</sub> = N<sub>A</sub>/k<sub>y</sub>. Across the liquid film, y<sub>i</sub> − y* = m(x<sub>i</sub> − x) = m N<sub>A</sub>/k<sub>x</sub>. Add and compare with N<sub>A</sub> = K<sub>y</sub>(y − y*).

blocks.where: K<sub>y</sub> is the overall gas coefficient, kmol/(m²·s); k<sub>y</sub> is the gas-film coefficient, kmol/(m²·s); k<sub>x</sub> is the liquid-film coefficient, kmol/(m²·s); m is the slope of y* = m x, dimensionless.

blocks.text: On the liquid basis, x* − x<sub>i</sub> = (y − y<sub>i</sub>)/m = N<sub>A</sub>/(m k<sub>y</sub>) and x<sub>i</sub> − x = N<sub>A</sub>/k<sub>x</sub>. Add and compare with N<sub>A</sub> = K<sub>x</sub>(x* − x).

blocks.where: K<sub>x</sub> is the overall liquid coefficient, kmol/(m²·s); the gas term 1/(m k<sub>y</sub>) converts gas-film resistance to the x basis; the liquid term 1/k<sub>x</sub> is the liquid-film resistance.

blocks.text: The factor m converts one phase's composition to the other phase's basis. The two overall coefficients are linked by K<sub>x</sub> = m K<sub>y</sub>. Use K<sub>y</sub> when the gas composition is measured; use K<sub>x</sub> when the liquid composition is measured. Never mix Δy and Δx in one sum.

When the equilibrium line is curved, m in 1/K<sub>y</sub> = 1/k<sub>y</sub> + m/k<sub>x</sub> is the slope m′ of the chord from (x, y*) to (x<sub>i</sub>, y<sub>i</sub>), and m in 1/K<sub>x</sub> is the slope m″ of the chord from (x<sub>i</sub>, y<sub>i</sub>) to (x*, y). A single m is exact only for a straight line. On a partial-pressure and liquid-concentration basis, with Henry's law p = H C, the same sum reads 1/K<sub>G</sub> = 1/k<sub>G</sub> + H/k<sub>L</sub>.

Resistance is 1/coefficient. The gas-film share of the resistance behind K<sub>y</sub> is (1/k<sub>y</sub>)/(1/K<sub>y</sub>). The liquid-film share is (m/k<sub>x</sub>)/(1/K<sub>y</sub>). The same percentages apply to K<sub>x</sub> because K<sub>x</sub> = m K<sub>y</sub>. If one share is above about 80%, that film controls. Gas-film control means extra liquid mixing gives little gain; increase gas velocity or gas turbulence. Liquid-film control means improve liquid mixing or add a reaction. In the worked example the gas film has 51.6 %, so neither film controls; both must be kept in the design. Watch m, not 1/k<sub>x</sub> alone. For a very soluble gas, m is small, so m/k<sub>x</sub> is small and the gas film often controls. For a sparingly soluble gas, m is large, so the liquid term often controls. A scrubber can therefore be gas-film controlled for ammonia and liquid-film controlled for carbon dioxide.

figure.caption: The worked example. Top: the gas-film resistance 20.0 and the liquid-film resistance on the gas basis, m/k<sub>x</sub> = 18.75, add like resistors to 1/K<sub>y</sub> = 38.75. Bottom: at y = 0.10 and x = 0.02 the solute mole fraction falls through the gas film to y<sub>i</sub> = 0.0639, jumps to x<sub>i</sub> = 0.0426 at the interface, where the phases are in equilibrium, and falls through the liquid film to 0.020.

examples.question: A solute is absorbed from a gas into a liquid. The individual coefficients are k<sub>y</sub> = 0.050 kmol/(m²·s) and k<sub>x</sub> = 0.080 kmol/(m²·s), each per unit mole-fraction difference, and the equilibrium line is y* = 1.5x. At one point in the column the bulk gas has y = 0.10 and the bulk liquid x = 0.02. Find K<sub>y</sub>, K<sub>x</sub>, the gas-film share of the resistance, the flux and the interface compositions.
steps: Liquid-film resistance on the gas basis = m/k<sub>x</sub> = 1.5/0.080 = 18.75 m²·s/kmol.
Overall driving force: y* = 1.5 × 0.02 = 0.030, so N<sub>A</sub> = K<sub>y</sub>(y − y*) = 0.0258 × (0.10 − 0.030) = 1.81×10⁻³ kmol/(m²·s).
Interface: y<sub>i</sub> = y − N<sub>A</sub>/k<sub>y</sub> = 0.10 − 1.81×10⁻³/0.050 = 0.0639, and x<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>/1.5 = 0.0426.
Check on the liquid side: k<sub>x</sub>(x<sub>i</sub> − x) = 0.080 × (0.0426 − 0.020) = 1.81×10⁻³ kmol/(m²·s). With x* = y/m = 0.0667, K<sub>x</sub>(x* − x) = 0.0387 × 0.0467 = 1.81×10⁻³ as well.
examples.answer: K<sub>y</sub> = 0.0258 and K<sub>x</sub> = 0.0387 kmol/(m²·s); the gas film carries 51.6 % of the resistance. The flux is 1.81×10⁻³ kmol/(m²·s), with y<sub>i</sub> = 0.0639 and x<sub>i</sub> = 0.0426.
examples.check:
ky = 0.05
kx = 0.08
m = 1.5
Ry = 1 / ky
Rx = m / kx
Ky = 1 / (Ry + Rx)
Kx = 1 / (1 / (m * ky) + 1 / kx)
share = Ry / (Ry + Rx) * 100
print(round(Ky, 4))
print(round(Kx, 4))
print(round(share, 1))

traps: For 1/K<sub>y</sub> the liquid term is m/k<sub>x</sub>. For 1/K<sub>x</sub> the gas term is 1/(m k<sub>y</sub>). Reversing m is the commonest error.
Do not add 1/k<sub>y</sub> and 1/k<sub>x</sub> directly. They sit on different driving forces. Convert with m first.
K<sub>y</sub> and K<sub>x</sub> have different numerical values and different driving-force bases. A resistance fraction must use the same basis as the coefficient.
m is the slope of y* = m x. If the equilibrium line is curved, use the chord slopes m′ (for K<sub>y</sub>) and m″ (for K<sub>x</sub>); a single m is valid only for a straight line.
The interface is in equilibrium, not the bulk phases. y* = m x uses the bulk liquid x, not the interface x<sub>i</sub>.

quiz.q: Define k<sub>y</sub> and K<sub>y</sub> with their driving forces.
quiz.a: k<sub>y</sub> = N<sub>A</sub>/(y − y<sub>i</sub>) is the gas-film coefficient. K<sub>y</sub> = N<sub>A</sub>/(y − y*) is the overall gas coefficient, with y* = m x.

quiz.q: Why is the liquid term in 1/K<sub>y</sub> multiplied by m?
quiz.a: The liquid driving force x<sub>i</sub> − x must be converted to a gas driving force: y<sub>i</sub> − y* = m(x<sub>i</sub> − x). With the same flux, this gives the term m/k<sub>x</sub>.

quiz.q: k<sub>y</sub> = 0.040 kmol/(m²·s), k<sub>x</sub> = 0.10 kmol/(m²·s), and m = 2.0. Find K<sub>y</sub>.
In the worked example, m rises to 3.0 while k<sub>y</sub> and k<sub>x</sub> stay fixed. Find the gas-film share in K<sub>y</sub> and state which film controls.
quiz.a: 1/k<sub>y</sub> = 20 and m/k<sub>x</sub> = 3.0/0.080 = 37.5, so 1/K<sub>y</sub> = 57.5 and K<sub>y</sub> = 0.0174 kmol/(m²·s). Gas share = 20/57.5 = 34.8 %, liquid share 65.2 %. Neither film passes the 80 % mark, but the liquid film now carries the larger share, so liquid-side improvements pay more than before.

quiz.q: Show that K<sub>x</sub> = m K<sub>y</sub> from the two resistance sums.
quiz.a: 1/K<sub>x</sub> = 1/(m k<sub>y</sub>) + 1/k<sub>x</sub> = (1/m)(1/k<sub>y</sub> + m/k<sub>x</sub>) = (1/m)(1/K<sub>y</sub>). Invert: K<sub>x</sub> = m K<sub>y</sub>.

quiz.q: An overall gas coefficient is K<sub>y</sub> = 0.020 kmol/(m²·s), and the gas film is 60% of the total resistance. Find k<sub>y</sub>.
What does using the same driving-force basis mean?
quiz.a: Every resistance term in one equation must use the same composition difference, either Δy or Δx. Convert the other phase with m before adding.

quiz.q: If K<sub>y</sub> = 0.025 kmol/(m²·s) and m = 1.5, find K<sub>x</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. Plant engineers rate existing absorbers from sampled y and x by back-calculating K<sub>y</sub>. Packed-tower software turns K<sub>y</sub> a into the height of a transfer unit (HTU), the packed height that gives one unit of composition change per unit of mean driving force. Search: overall gas-phase mass transfer coefficient, gas-film versus liquid-film control.
